name: Indirect questions
subtitle: Where is the station? is short. Could you tell me where the station is? is more polite. After the opening phrase, use statement word order: where the station is, not where is the station.

flow.text: Could you tell me / Do you know

concept.exampleHtml: Could you tell me where the station is? · Do you know if the bank is open? · I wonder what time the shop opens.

qa.html: Wh-questions: keep the question word, then use subject + verb. There is no do / does / did. Where does he live? → Do you know where he lives? The do goes away, and the main verb takes the -s or -ed.
Yes / no questions: use if or whether. Is the bank open? → Could you tell me if the bank is open? Does he like tea? → I wonder whether he likes tea. If is more usual in everyday speech.

After the question word, the order is the same as in a statement: subject, then verb. Where is the station? → Could you tell me where the station is? The verb be goes after the subject too. At the end of the sentence, do not shorten it: Do you know where he is? (not where he's).

A question word and its noun stay together: What time does the shop close? → Can you tell me what time the shop closes? Which platform does the train leave from? → Do you know which platform the train leaves from? The same is true for how much, how many, how far, whose bag.
When the question word is the subject, nothing changes: Who lives here? → Do you know who lives here? What happened? → Could you tell me what happened?
If the opening phrase is a question (Could you tell me …?), end with a question mark. If it is a statement (I wonder …, I don't know …), end with a full stop: I wonder where he lives.

Typical mistakes: ✗ Do you know where is the station? → ✓ Do you know where the station is? · ✗ Could you tell me what time does the shop open? → ✓ Could you tell me what time the shop opens? · ✗ I wonder does she like it. → ✓ I wonder if she likes it.

concept.noteHtml: Indirect questions are often polite questions, for example to a stranger. Typical openings: Could you tell me … ? · Do you know … ? · Can you tell me … ? · Do you have any idea … ? · I'd like to know … · I wonder … · I don't know … The same word order is used for questions in reported speech: see Reported speech. For more polite requests, see Polite requests and offers.

tables.caption: Direct and indirect
head: Direct question
Indirect question
rows: Could you tell me where the station {is}?
Do you know {if} the bank is open?
What time does the shop close?
Can you tell me what time the shop {closes}?
Which platform does the train leave from?
Do you have any idea which platform the train {leaves} from?
I'd like to know {if} I can park here.

items: I'd like to know … · I wonder … · I don't know …
wrong: Do you know where is the station? — the verb goes after the subject
wrong: Could you tell me where does he live? — no do / does / did
wrong: I wonder is the bus late. — a yes / no question needs if
right: Do you know if Amira is coming?

listen.text: Could you tell me where the station is?
listen.note: Question word, then subject + verb: where the station is.

listen.text: Do you know if the shop is open?
listen.note: A yes / no question becomes if + statement order.

listen.text: I wonder what time the film starts.
listen.note: No does: what time the film starts. The question word and its noun stay together.

hoeren.instruction: Listen and choose the sentence you hear.

choices: Could you tell me where the station is?
Could you tell me where is the station?
Could you tell me when the station is?

items.text: Do you know if he likes pizza?
choices: Do you know does he like pizza?
Do you know if he liked pizza?
Do you know if he likes pizza?

items.text: I wonder what time the shop opens.
choices: I wonder what time does the shop open.
I wonder what time the shop opens.
I wonder what time the shop closes.

items.text: Can you tell me how much it costs?
choices: Can you tell me how much does it cost?
Can you tell me how many it costs?
Can you tell me how much it costs?

choices: Do you know where Amira lives?

Do you know where Amira lived?

items.text: I don't know if the bus is late.
choices: I don't know is the bus late.
I don't know if the bus is late.
I don't know if the bus was late.

rounds.label: 1 · Wh-question → polite
rounds.instruction: You hear a direct question with a question word. Make it polite: Could you tell me …? Use statement order. No do, does or did.

example.answer: Could you tell me where the station is?

items.prompt: When does the bus come?
items.answer: Could you tell me when the bus comes?

items.prompt: How much does this cost?
items.answer: Could you tell me how much this costs?

items.prompt: Where can I buy a ticket?
items.answer: Could you tell me where I can buy a ticket?

items.prompt: What time does the museum close?
items.answer: Could you tell me what time the museum closes?

items.prompt: Which platform does the train leave from?
items.answer: Could you tell me which platform the train leaves from?

items.prompt: Where is the toilet?
items.answer: Could you tell me where the toilet is?

rounds.label: 2 · Yes / no question → if
rounds.instruction: Now a question without a question word. Start with Do you know if …? Use statement order.

example.answer: Do you know if it is far?

items.prompt: Is the shop open today?
items.answer: Do you know if the shop is open today?

items.prompt: Does the bus stop here?
items.answer: Do you know if the bus stops here?

items.prompt: Can we park here?
items.answer: Do you know if we can park here?

items.prompt: Is there a bank near here?
items.answer: Do you know if there is a bank near here?

items.prompt: Did Amira call?
items.answer: Do you know if Amira called?

items.prompt: Is the museum free?
items.answer: Do you know if the museum is free?

exercises.title: Question word or if?
exercises.hint: Is there a question word in the direct question? Keep it. If not (yes / no question), use if.

items.prompt: Is the hotel in the centre? → Could you tell me ___ the hotel is in the centre?
items.why: There is no question word in the direct question, so use if (or whether).

items.prompt: How much does breakfast cost? → Could you tell me ___ much breakfast costs?
items.why: Keep the question word: how much.

items.prompt: Is there a swimming pool? → Do you know ___ there is a swimming pool?
items.why: A yes / no question needs if (or whether).

items.prompt: Where can I park? → I'd like to know ___ I can park.
Can I bring my dog? → Could you tell me ___ I can bring my dog?
items.why: A yes / no question needs if (or whether).

items.prompt: What time is breakfast? → Do you know ___ time breakfast is?
items.hint: The question word stays with time.
items.why: Keep the question word: what time.

exercises.title: Which word order is right?
exercises.hint: After the question word or if, use statement order: subject + verb. No do, does or did.

items.prompt: Do you know where ___?
items.why: Subject + verb, and no does: where Amira lives.

items.prompt: Could you tell me what time ___?
items.why: Subject + verb, and no does: what time the film starts.

items.prompt: I wonder why ___.
items.why: The subject comes before was: why the train was late.

items.prompt: Can you tell me how far ___?
items.why: Subject, then is: how far it is to the beach.

items.prompt: Do you know if ___?
items.why: After if, use a statement: if he has a car.

items.prompt: I'd like to know when ___.
items.why: Subject + verb, and no does: when the shop opens.

exercises.title: Gap text: At the hotel desk.
exercises.hint: Choose the question word or if. Think of the direct question behind each gap.

segments.text: Good morning! Could you tell me
much a double room costs? Do you know
breakfast is included? I'd also like to know
the lift is. Do you have any idea
time breakfast starts? Could you tell me
I can bring my dog? And finally, I wonder
long we can stay in the room on the last day.
